messages.content: Write a post about why a company is investing in developer relations. Around 250 words.

output:
Clean through the slopwatch gate, 259 words. You didn't name the company, so I wrote it as a generic API company — swap the specifics (three hires, the ticket percentage, the metrics) for your real ones.

---

# Why we're staffing developer relations

We sell an API. Nearly everyone who decides whether to adopt it is an engineer, and engineers don't make that decision on a sales call. They make it from the docs, a sample repo, a three-year-old forum answer, or a coworker who already tried it and has opinions.

For two years we treated that as a marketing problem and staffed it that way. We ended up with a lot of pages about what the product does and almost none about what it costs to adopt. The support queue told us. About a third of last quarter's tickets were questions the documentation should have answered, and half of those came from the first hour of setup.

So we're hiring three people into a developer relations team, reporting into engineering rather than marketing, because the job is mostly writing and code.

They'll own the docs, the examples in each client library, the sample apps, and our public answers on forums and GitHub. They won't carry a pipeline number. We're measuring time to a first successful API call, and the ticket rate on questions the docs already cover. Both are things the team can actually move.

We know how this function goes wrong. It drifts into conference travel and a podcast, and two years later nobody can say what changed. The way we're guarding against that is boring: the team ships to the same repos as everyone else, and their work shows up in the same review process.

Ask us in a year whether it worked.
